title: Can Both Knees Be Replaced at the Same Time? Safety, Risks and Alternatives
metaDescription: Is bilateral knee replacement in one sitting safe? What the evidence says on heart risk, infection, recovery and staging, from an orthopaedic surgeon in Thane.
intro: "Can we do both knees together, so I only go through this once?" is one of the most common questions from people with arthritis in both knees. It is a reasonable wish, and for some patients it works well. It also carries extra risks that a single-knee operation does not, so the honest answer is "it depends on your heart and lungs". This guide sets out what the research shows and how to choose.

sections.heading: Is it safe to have both knees replaced at the same time?
sections.body:
For carefully selected patients with a healthy heart and lungs, it can be reasonable, but it is a bigger physiological load than one knee, and it is not the right choice for everyone. A pooled analysis of earlier studies linked simultaneous surgery with more cardiac and lung complications than staged surgery. That is why fitness checks come first.

The evidence is retrospective, so it shows associations, not proof. It cannot tell us exactly which patient is safe, which is why the decision is individual.

sections.heading: What are the main risks of doing both knees together?
sections.body:
The main extra risks are cardiac and lung events, including heart attack and blood clots reaching the lungs, plus a longer operation and more blood loss. A 2007 meta-analysis in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery found simultaneous bilateral replacement was associated with higher rates of pulmonary embolism, cardiac complications and death than staged surgery, and staged outcomes were similar to a single knee.

A large retrospective US study presented at the 2011 AAOS meeting also reported more heart attacks and pulmonary embolism within 30 days after simultaneous surgery, with similar death and stroke rates. For any single knee replacement, OrthoInfo says serious complications occur in fewer than 2% of patients and blood clots in the leg veins are among the most common.

sections.heading: Does doing both knees together have any advantages?
sections.body:
Yes: one anaesthetic, one hospital stay and one rehabilitation period. For many families in Thane and Mumbai, taking leave from work once and arranging help once matters. The same US study found fewer serious joint infections needing another operation after simultaneous surgery (1.2% versus 2.2% for staged), though this was a conference presentation and an association, not a guarantee.

On cost, the figures on this site are indicative only: roughly Rs 1.5 to 2 lakh per knee for traditional replacement and Rs 2.5 to 3 lakh per knee for robotic. Doing both together saves one set of hospital and anaesthesia charges, but the total is still higher than for one knee, and the written estimate follows assessment.

sections.heading: Who should not have both knees done together?
sections.body:
People with heart disease, poorly controlled diabetes or blood pressure, significant lung disease, a past blood clot, or severe frailty are usually better served by staging. The US researchers concluded that simultaneous surgery is probably best kept for patients at low risk of cardiovascular complications, and said more research is needed to define who should not have it.

This is also a good reason to have a physician and anaesthetist review you beforehand, and to be wary of any clinic that offers both knees to everyone without asking about your heart.

sections.heading: If we stage it, how far apart should the two operations be?
sections.body:
There is no agreed interval. The 2007 meta-analysis could not identify a gap that removes the extra risk. A 2024 Indian hospital newsletter describes staged surgery as two operations about 48 hours apart, while many surgeons wait months so the first knee recovers fully. Both are used in practice.

The choice depends on how much the worse knee limits you, how fit you are, and whether you can manage one weak leg at a time. If the second knee is only mildly symptomatic, some people find it settles after the first is replaced, and it can be reviewed later.

sections.heading: How is recovery different when both knees are done?
sections.body:
It is more demanding. With both legs sore and weak at once, getting up, using the toilet and climbing stairs need more help and a longer plan, and rehabilitation can feel slower at first. OrthoInfo notes that after knee replacement most people can walk with a stick or walker soon after surgery but need help for several weeks with cooking, shopping and bathing.

Plan for a helper at home, a ground-floor arrangement if stairs are a problem, and a clear physiotherapy schedule. Our single-knee timeline is a starting point only; with both knees, expect to be at the slower end.

faqs.q: Can both knees be replaced in one surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, for medically fit patients, both knees can be replaced under one anaesthetic. It gives one hospital stay and one recovery period, but it is a larger physiological demand than one knee, so cardiac and general fitness are assessed first.

faqs.q: Is bilateral knee replacement riskier than doing one knee at a time?
faqs.a: For some risks, yes. Pooled studies associate simultaneous surgery with more cardiac and lung complications, including pulmonary embolism, than staged surgery. The evidence is retrospective, so it shows association, and risk depends heavily on your own health.

faqs.q: Who should not have both knees replaced together?
faqs.a: People with heart disease, significant lung disease, a past blood clot, poorly controlled diabetes or blood pressure, or frailty are usually better staged. Researchers suggest simultaneous surgery suits patients at low cardiovascular risk.

faqs.q: How long should I wait between the two knee replacements if staged?
faqs.a: There is no agreed interval, and studies have not found a gap that removes the extra risk. Some units operate about 48 hours apart, while many surgeons wait months. Your surgeon will advise based on your fitness and symptoms.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to do both knees together?
faqs.a: Per knee, usually yes, because you pay for one hospital stay and one anaesthetic. The total is still higher than for a single knee. Figures on this site are indicative only, around Rs 1.5 to 2 lakh per knee traditional and Rs 2.5 to 3 lakh robotic, and a written estimate follows assessment.

footerNote: If both knees hurt, an assessment with standing X-rays and a fitness review will show whether doing them together, staging them, or waiting is sensible. Read about knee replacement, whether you can delay it, cost in Thane and insurance cover, or book a consultation. Sudden chest pain, breathlessness, or a swollen painful calf after any knee surgery needs emergency care.
